name: Brazilian Galinhada (Chicken and Saffron Rice)
writer_notes: SELECTOR: Page verified: full recipe, 5 servings, 738 cal / 33g protein - the highest-calorie candidate in the slice and comfortably over both bars as written. One-pot chicken-and-rice, and the source gives an electric-pressure-cooker variant that suits large batches. Saffron unmapped but the dish works on tracked ground-turmeric, which the recipe already lists. Confidence: high. | HARVEST: The recipe card served on this URL is PORTUGUESE ONLY - confirmed on a second fetch asking specifically for an English card. Ingredient lines are transcribed verbatim in Portuguese and will need translation downstream. Servings published as '5 pessoas'. Line 1 = 1 kg bone-in skin-on chicken thighs (about 4-5).
OVERRIDE Rice: Portuguese card: '2 xicaras de arroz' = 2 cups dry rice
OVERRIDE Vegetable Oil: Portuguese card: '2 colheres de sopa' = 2 tbsp
OVERRIDE Diced Tomatoes: Portuguese card: '3 tomates grandes' = 3 large FRESH tomatoes, not cans
OVERRIDE Frozen Green Peas: Portuguese card: '3/4 xicara de ervilhas' = 3/4 cup
intro_html: Galinhada is Brazil's answer to arroz con pollo, and it comes from Minas Gerais, where they cook it in one big pot for a crowd and everyone eats standing up. Chicken browns first, then the rice cooks in the drippings and the broth until it turns golden and every grain has picked up flavor. Peas and scallions go on at the end for color. Each bowl runs 662 calories and 50 grams of protein for about $3.25 (at everyday cost). One pot, no fuss, fourteen dinners.
ingredients_display: Boneless Skinless Chicken Thigh (Member's Mark): 6.25 lb (2800 g)
cost_note_html: Real Omaha store prices from our weekly grocery board (2026). They still swing by store and by what is on sale.
cost_lines: Boneless Skinless Chicken Thigh, 6.25 lb: ~$10.93. Buy 7 lbs: $12.39.
Rice, 5.75 cups dry: ~$1.28. Pantry staple; this batch alone uses about 2 2lb bags.
Chicken Broth, 2.5 cartons: ~$3.16. Pantry staple; this batch alone uses about 3 32oz cartons.
Lemon Juice, 1.4 lemons worth: ~$0.25. Buy 1 (lasts several batches).
Pantry seasonings (bay leaves): ~$0.28. From jars you keep on hand.

Batch total: about $27.31 across 14 servings, so roughly $1.95 per bowl. This counts only the amounts this batch actually uses from each package, so it is the cost of the food in the containers, not a register receipt.

True shopping cost: about $30.07 across 14 servings, roughly $2.15 per bowl. What the register trip looks like if your pantry is already stocked. Meat, produce, and packaged items are counted as the whole packages you have to buy, since you cannot grab a partial box, can, or jar. Pantry staples you already own (rice, seasonings, oils, and long-lasting sauces) are counted at only what this batch uses.

Starting with an empty pantry? Add about $8.32 one time. That is the extra cost of buying full containers of every pantry staple in this recipe instead of just the amounts used, which puts a first shopping trip near $38.39. Those containers then feed this batch and many more after it.
cost_closing_html: About $3.25 a bowl (at everyday cost) for a one-pot chicken and rice that eats like a party dish. The chicken is the biggest line by a distance and the rice underneath barely registers on the receipt.
shop_smart: Buy rice in the biggest bag you can store. It is the cheapest calorie in this recipe by a mile, it never goes bad, and every one-pot dish on this site leans on it.
Tomato paste in small cans is cheaper per ounce than the tube, and this recipe uses about three cans worth, so you will not be throwing away a half-used tube.
Frozen peas beat canned on price, color and texture. A single twelve ounce bag covers this batch for pocket change and the rest of the bag keeps in the freezer indefinitely.
Green bell peppers cost less than red almost every week of the year, and this dish traditionally uses green, so there is nothing to trade away.
make_it: Weigh your empty mixing pot and write the number down for portioning later.
Cut the chicken thighs into large pieces and season them with the lemon juice. Let them sit 20 minutes while you chop everything else.

Heat the vegetable oil in your largest heavy pot over medium-high and brown the chicken in batches until it has real color on both sides. Do not rush this, because the fond on the bottom of the pot is the entire flavor base. Set the chicken aside.
Cook the diced onion and green bell pepper in the same pot for 5 minutes, then add the garlic and the tomato paste and cook 2 more minutes until the paste turns brick red.
Stir in the dry rice and toast it for 2 minutes so every grain gets coated in the tomato and the drippings.
Add the diced tomatoes, chicken broth and bay leaves, then nestle the chicken back in with all its juices and bring the pot to a boil.
Drop to the lowest heat, cover tightly, and cook 20 to 25 minutes without lifting the lid, until the rice is tender and the chicken reads 165F.
Scatter the frozen peas over the top, re-cover, and let it sit off the heat 10 minutes. Then pull the bay leaves, fluff from the bottom, and fold in the sliced green onions.
portion_html: Set the loaded pot on the scale, subtract the empty-pot weight, and divide by 14. Same scoop in every container. Each one carries 662 calories, and a splash of water before reheating brings the rice back to where it started.

recipeIngredient: Boneless Skinless Chicken Thigh, 6.25 lb (2800 g)
steps: Season the cut chicken with the lemon juice and rest 20 minutes.
Brown the chicken in oil in batches, then set aside and soften onion and bell pepper with garlic and tomato paste.
Toast the dry rice in the pot for 2 minutes.
Add tomatoes, broth and bay leaves, return the chicken, cover, and cook on low 20 to 25 minutes.
Add peas off the heat for 10 minutes, fluff with green onions, and portion into 14 containers.
